mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a new flexible denture to feel tight?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, some degree of tightness or awareness is entirely normal in the early weeks of wearing a new flexible denture. Your gum tissues are adapting to the presence of the appliance, and daily tissue fluctuations can make the fit feel slightly variable. Most patients find that comfort improves over the first few weeks as the tissues settle. However, if tightness is significant, painful, or does not improve with time, it is worth arranging a review appointment with your dental team so that the fit can be professionally assessed.

mainEntity.name: Can my diet affect how my flexible denture fits?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, dietary choices can have a modest influence on how your flexible denture feels throughout the day. Foods high in sodium can cause fluid retention, which may contribute to mild soft tissue swelling by the evening. Staying well hydrated and maintaining a balanced diet can support more consistent tissue volume. If you notice that particular foods consistently worsen the tightness, making a note of this and discussing it with your dentist can help to identify any contributing patterns worth addressing.

mainEntity.name: Should I remove my flexible denture at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, yes. Removing your flexible denture overnight gives the gum tissues an opportunity to rest and reduces the risk of conditions such as denture-related stomatitis. Your dental team will advise you on the most appropriate wearing schedule based on your individual circumstances. Overnight removal also allows you to soak and clean the denture thoroughly, supporting good oral and appliance hygiene. Always follow the specific aftercare advice given by your dental professional, as individual recommendations may vary.

mainEntity.name: How often should a flexible denture be reviewed?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is generally advisable to have your denture and oral tissues reviewed at least once a year, though your dental team may recommend more frequent appointments depending on your individual needs and how your tissues are changing. Denture fit should be assessed regularly because the underlying jawbone and gum tissue naturally change shape over time following tooth loss. Early identification of fit issues allows for timely adjustments and helps to prevent complications such as pressure sores or accelerated bone resorption.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my flexible denture is causing sore spots?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your flexible denture is creating persistent sore spots or ulcers on your gum tissue, contact your dental team to arrange a review. Sore spots are a relatively common issue in the early stages of denture wear and often improve with minor chairside adjustments to the denture border. Avoid attempting to adjust the denture yourself, as this can cause further damage to the appliance or your tissues. In the meantime, removing the denture for short rest periods during the day may provide some relief, but professional assessment is recommended.

mainEntity.name: Will my flexible denture need replacing over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, flexible dentures do not last indefinitely. Over time, changes to the shape of the jawbone and gum tissues following tooth loss mean that even a well-fitting denture may gradually become less well-adapted to the oral anatomy. Most flexible dentures are expected to require replacement or significant reline after a number of years, though this varies between individuals. Regular dental reviews help to monitor when a new denture or adjustment may be needed. Your dental team can advise you on the expected lifespan of your specific appliance based on clinical assessment.
